justification: We measured Medline's per share equity value using two independent methods - a five year DCF and a comparable company analysis and then triangulated them to arrive at a defensible range. justification: Both DCF models were built specifically for cross border projects where cash flows originate in Argentina but serve global markets. I set the WACC at 9% to reflect the higher risk profile of emerging market investments compared to developed market benchmarks, following the principle that discount rates must be adjusted for country specific risk in multinational capital budgeting (Madura, 2003). For the hydrogen project, I addressed currency exposure by noting that export revenues would be denominated in EUR/USD, creating a natural hedge against Argentine peso depreciation - a technique discussed in Bodnar (1980) as one of the most effective ways to manage FX risk without costly financial instruments. The sensitivity tables stress testing WACC from 7% to 12% were designed to show how the NPV of each project responds to changes in the cost of capital, which is the central question when evaluating global investments where political, regulatory, and macroeconomic conditions can shift the required return.

title: The WM Wrigley Jr Company: Capital Structure, Valuation, and Cost of Capital
justification: This entire paper is fundamentally a capital structure optimization exercise, and we analyzed it from multiple angles rather than relying on a single framework. We started with APV and the MM tax shield ($1.2B at $3B debt) in Q1, then showed in Q2 that WACC stays flat under pure MM - basically confirming that the standard WACC approach cannot differentiate between debt levels for this firm. In Q3 we layered on trade off theory by estimating expected distress costs using Warner (1977) for direct costs, Andrade and Kaplan (1998) for indirect costs, and S&P/Altman default data for probability of default, arriving at net value creation of $680M at $3B. Then in Q5 we built a variable Kd model using Exhibit 7 yields by rating (AAA at 9.3% up to CCC at 18%) to finally produce the theoretical U shaped WACC curve, which bottoms at $1.25B (Exhibit A5). We stress tested our $2.4B recommendation against both $1.25B and $3B across multiple dimensions - coverage ratios, EBIT decline thresholds (-25% kills $3B, -40% kills $2.4B, while $1.25B survives -60%), Wrigley adjusted default probabilities, and distress cost ranges from 10% to 25% (Exhibits A3, A5, A6). The final recommendation synthesizes all of these into a single debt level that balances tax efficiency, distress risk and strategic control for a mature consumer staple.

title: The WM Wrigley Jr Company: Capital Structure, Valuation, and Cost of Capital
context: Wrigley Jr. Company Calculations GLOs & HCs to be scored This entire paper is fundamentally a capital structure optimization exercise, and we analyzed it from multiple angles rather than relying on a single framework.

title: The WM Wrigley Jr Company: Capital Structure, Valuation, and Cost of Capital
justification: We traced how leverage mechanically transforms every major financial metric for a mature, zero debt firm. EPS drops from $1.33 to $0.32 under dividends and $0.41 under repurchase (Exhibit A4), not because the business got worse but because $390M in annual interest expense now sits between EBIT and net income. WACC barely moves from 10.90% to 10.91% (Exhibit A2), which we explained through MM Proposition II - the rising cost of equity (from 10.9% to 11.7%) almost perfectly offsets the cheaper after tax debt (7.8%), so the discount rate is essentially unchanged. Book equity goes to -$1.7B, which looks alarming but is purely an accounting artifact since book value does not capture $13B in market value. Coverage drops to 1.3x at $3B debt, 1.66x at our recommended $2.4B. We didn’t want to just report these numbers so we built sensitivity tables (Exhibits A2, A4, A5) showing how each metric moves across debt levels from $0 to $4B, and across EBIT scenarios from worst to best case, so professor can see exactly where the inflection points are and why mature firm metrics behave differently under leverage than growth firm metrics would.

title: The WM Wrigley Jr Company: Capital Structure, Valuation, and Cost of Capital
justification: The entire recommendation in Q5 is built around strategic support. Instead of just picking the debt level that maximizes a formula output, we asked what capital structure decision actually supports the Wrigley family's long term enterprise strategy. The answer turned out to be $2.4B - not because it minimizes WACC (that would be $1.25B) and not because it maximizes expected value (that would be $3B+), but because it is the precise minimum debt needed to push family voting control from 46.6% to 50.1% through share repurchase. We calculated that repurchasing 43M common shares at $56.37 basically reduces total votes from 616M to 573M while the family's 287M votes stay intact (our Exhibit A6). That majority control threshold is the strategic foundation that protects a 100 year old brand from hostile activists like for example Aurora Borealis. The $970M tax shield and $4.14 per share value creation are the financial benefits, but our investment decision is ultimately grounded in what supports the enterprise's long term positioning and governance stability as well.

justification: The assignment asks one big question (should Wrigley recapitalize and if so, how much?) but we couldn’t answer this question without decomposing it into tractable parts. So we broke it into five sequential components, each with its own spreadsheet tab feeding into the next. Tab 1 (APV) isolates the pure tax shield value and establishes the baseline enterprise and equity values. Tab 2 (WACC) handles the cost of capital calculation separately so the discount rate mechanics do not get tangled with the valuation. Tab 3 (Distress Costs) subtracts expected bankruptcy costs from the tax shield to get net value creation - this required breaking the problem further into sub components: like estimating distress cost as a percentage of firm value, mapping coverage ratios to credit ratings via Exhibit 6 like we did, pulling default probabilities from academic data, and then multiplying through. Tab 4 (Dividend vs Repurchase) isolates the payout mechanism decision from the debt level decision, analyzing EPS, voting control, and tax implications independently. And then Tab 5 (Optimal Debt) pulls everything together with a comprehensive scenario table across nine debt levels from $0 to $4B, and Tab 6 (Majority Control) solves for the exact debt amount ($2.4B) that achieves the 50.1% voting threshold. Each component is solvable on its own, but the final recommendation only works because all six pieces connect - the APV feeds the WACC weights, the distress costs adjust the APV, the repurchase analysis informs the payout choice and the optimal debt table frames the final recommendation.

title: Deep Dive: Vector Space Structure
justification: Organize problems into tractable components and design solutions. I applied this HC throughout the whole assignment but especially in Questions 3 and 4. The lossy compression problem sounds complicated when you first read it but I broke it down into smaller steps that were each pretty manageable on their own. For example in Q3 instead of trying to do everything at once I first focused on just finding the coordinates of v in the new basis (which is really just doing dot products like I practiced in class). Then separately I dealt with the thresholding part where I set small coordinates to zero. And then converting back to the standard basis was its own step. Each piece on its own was not that hard but putting them together in the right order gave me the full compression pipeline. Same thing in Q4 when I extended to 2D. That felt like a big jump at first but I broke it down into: first build the image, then apply the 1D transform to each row, then apply it to each column, then do the thresholding, then reverse the whole process. Breaking it into those steps made it way more doable instead of trying to figure out the whole 2D case at once.

justification: ([NAME]): we analyzed Beck's cognitive model to explore how beliefs in astrology influence romantic choices; it explores the cognitive aspects of individuals who believe in astrology, the environmental factors like social and cultural influences that reinforce these beliefs, and the behaviors in result, such as for example consulting horoscopes. context: Beck, in creating his cognitive theory, asserts that behavior is an embodiment of an individual’s cognition, environmental factors, and their interconnected relationships. In this case, one’s cognitive state is modeled through analyses of thinking patterns and motivations, while their environment is composed of social and cultural influences. These two aspects then influence the behavioral aspect by prompting actions such as reading daily horoscope predictions, consulting astrological readings, and, eventually, making life choices based on these beliefs.

title: 'Irrational' Behavior Research Paper
justification: ([NAME]): we dissected this complex idea of believing in astrology by integrating multiple layers of analysis: individual, interpersonal, intrapersonal and societal. This shows how individual cognitive biases and social constructs interplay with broader societal influences in shaping one’s belief in astrology. Such multilevel analysis is crucial since it provides a view of different layers of the system and helps us understand how one influences another.
context: People who subscribe to the belief of astrology have the cognitive idea that celestial bodies' positions at birth can provide insights into a person's personality traits, hence, one person's compatibility with another's. While initially appearing irrational, it is deeply rooted in psychological needs, social constructs, and cognitive biases, serving a more complex purpose than exemplifying irrational behavior (Delgado, 2021). To examine this phenomenon, we propose applying Beck’s cognitive model: performing analyses on both an individual and societal level, then studying their interactions to see how they influence behavior.
